title: A Case Study on Parametric Verification of Failure Detectors
what: The authors model the Chandra-Toueg failure detector (a protocol that guesses which machines have crashed) in TLA+, Ivy and counter automata, assuming partial synchrony (the network is unpredictable at first, then becomes well-behaved). They prove liveness (something good eventually happens) by hand, turning it into a safety proof (nothing bad happens).
assumptions_limits: The conversion from liveness to safety is done by hand. Ivy's automatic conversion was not used.
use_for_goal: This is one of few machine-checked liveness proofs that assume partial synchrony and a GST (the global stabilization time, after which the network behaves).

quotes.text: we show how to verify liveness of the failure detector by reducing the verification problem to safety verification.

title: A Messy State of the Union: Taming the Composite State Machines of TLS
venue: IEEE S&P (CACM 2017 version cited by RFC2TLA+)
what: The authors test TLS libraries for state-machine bugs by generating traces that deviate from the allowed behavior. They also write a replacement C state machine for OpenSSL and prove in Frama-C that it only allows traces from a hand-written list of allowed traces. A Coq proof shows that two sides with equal handshake logs are in equal states.

title: Compositional Verification of Composite Byzantine Protocols
what: Embeds TLA in Coq and assumes that message delivery is weakly fair (a message that stays deliverable is eventually delivered). Proves that pending packets are eventually delivered and that protocol phases finish. The method: for each phase, find a finite set of packets that is enough. Show that delivering them starts the next phase. Chain the phases with the transitivity of the leads-to relation (for example init ∧ □next ∧ WFDelivery ⊢ sent ~~> output). Covers Provable Broadcast, Reliable Broadcast, Accountable Confirmer and Accountable Reliable Broadcast.
numbers: full development about 7100 Coq lines, trusted OCaml shim about 200
liveness spec/proof lines: Bythos library 160/181; Provable Broadcast 92/67; Reliable Broadcast 144/161; Accountable Confirmer 172/200; composition 3/7; connector 48/92
knowledge lemmas: 10-20 per case, found manually
assumptions_limits: Fairness holds only for delivery to honest processes. The set of honest members is fixed. No proof of probabilistic termination. Partial synchrony (bounded message delays that hold only after some unknown time) is left to future work. The combined proof is tiny only after humans find reusable interfaces and facts about the connectors. The paper does not state how long the authors took.
use_for_goal: Shows exactly how a user states the delivery assumption and the pending request in a proof.

title: The LAW theorem: Local Reads and Linearizable Asynchronous Replication
what: The paper proves that no replicated register can have all three of these: a local read (a read with no messages), linearizability, and a guarantee that operations finish despite async delays and one crash. It designs almost-local reads (batched read validation) in Hermes, ZAB and Raft variants.
numbers: Raft-ALR 2.6x baseline throughput at 2% writes, 1.8x at 5%; up to 156 million requests/s
ZAB-ALR within 4% of ZAB at 1% writes; Hermes-ALR within 11% at 1% writes
5 CloudLab servers, one million keys; reads batched up to 128
assumptions_limits: A human wrote a mathematical proof about a mathematical register (deterministic servers, one active operation each, at most one crash). The correctness of the read algorithms is argued in prose. The Raft baseline relaxes linearizability, so the performance comparison is an upper bound. There is no LLM, no code proof and no person-hours.
use_for_goal: The notes infer that a vague wish for fast local reads, strong consistency and crash tolerance needs an explicit answer on timing and progress. An agent should point out incompatible requirements and propose a checked alternative.

title: Lawyer: Modular Obligations-Based Liveness Reasoning in Higher-Order Impredicative Concurrent Separation Logic
what: Lawyer proves fair termination (every fairly scheduled run finishes) in Rocq/Iris. It uses a logical transition system of obligations. A well-founded hierarchy orders the dependencies to rule out cycles. assumptions_limits: Finite sets of levels limit lock-coupling structures that grow without bound. Progress for independent modules, and liveness of programs that never terminate, are future work. The notes found no effort count.
use_for_goal: Fair scheduling alone is not enough if a holder never unlocks. The contract must say so.

title: PVerifier (P language verification extensions)
what: It checks inductive proofs of designs written in the P language. Users supply assumptions and an inductive invariant. title: Reasoning about Weak Isolation Levels in Separation Logic
what: The paper writes transaction specs that do not depend on the implementation, for read-uncommitted, read-committed and snapshot isolation. It proves that known bad histories are prohibited. It verifies an in-memory, single-node MVCC key-value database, accessed over RPC, in OCaml/Aneris.
assumptions_limits: It covers a single node, with no replication or crash recovery. The review did not verify the translator from source to AnerisLang or the runtime.
use_for_goal: It gives several meanings of "transactions are correct". It also shows how to test a spec against known anomalies.

quotes.text: All results are mechanized in the Rocq proof assistant on top of the Iris separation logic framework.

title: What's Live? Understanding Distributed Consensus

title: Automated Verification of Safety and Liveness Properties for Distributed Protocols (PhD thesis)
what: It shows that liveness can be reduced to a list of simpler safety properties, which invariant-inference tools often prove automatically. One task is left: synthesize a ranking function (a number that decreases toward the goal) to prove termination. It was applied to 8 protocols, including Paxos. It also covers DistAI and DuoAI.
numbers: 37 of 40 generated safety properties are always true, inductive, or get an invariant automatically; 3 found manually in a few hours each
every Z3 query to synthesize a ranking function finished in under a second
manual effort 128 and 165 lines versus IronFleet's 2,093 and 7,869 lines of Dafny (16x and 47x less)
DuoAI covers 27 protocols and solves Paxos more than two orders of magnitude faster than any alternative
assumptions_limits: It handles only "eventually" properties, not bounded time. Ranking functions are polynomials only. It works on protocol-level models, not code. It assumes fair scheduling, minimum packet delivery and a contention-free Paxos round. Part of the line-count gap is Dafny versus mypyvy. The notes' author read about 20% of the 137 pages.
use_for_goal: It shows liveness can be partly automated. The human hints still needed (extra variables, bounds, contradictions) are a target for an agent.

quotes.text: liveness verification can be soundly reduced to the verification of a list of simpler safety properties, which can often be proved automatically utilizing an arsenal of invariant inference tools. The reduction leaves one remaining task - to synthesize a ranking function to prove termination.
In most cases, Z3 synthesizes the exact same ranking function as a human would manually specify.

quotes.text: We have formally verified ZENITH's specifications and have proved that it ensures the network state will eventually be consistent with intent. We automatically generate ZENITH's code from its specification.
